Issued at 1143 PM CDT Tue Sep 15 2026

Today and Tomorrow

Water vapor imagery this evening features broad southwesterly 
flow across the majority of the CONUS, lobbed eastward by a 
digging trough pushing inland from the Pacific Coast. Zooming in
locally, we find ourselves to the north of a cold front draped 
from western Oklahoma towards central Illinois, with broad warm 
air advection and isentropic lift overrunning that boundary to 
extend shower development northward. Working with those broader 
lift mechanisms are localized pockets of low-level frontogenesis
that have allowed some of the elevated storms reach their full 
potential across northern Missouri. Along and north of the 
frontal boundary, precipitable water values are at their peak of
2+ inches to go with long/skinny instability profiles that are 
supportive of warm rain processes. This environment will expand 
into southeastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa, with MCVs 
developed by the convection and subtle zones of frontogenesis 
being the things to track for heavy rainfall monitoring. Healthy
rainfall amounts are expected out of established storms, with 
wetter soils making flooding an increased risk through noon 
tomorrow when shower and storm activity slows. River basins so 
far have behaved aside from some minor flooding along the East 
Nishnabotna River near Red Oak, but focused rain in across the 
southeastern forecast area would give us more hydro-related 
headaches in the short-term. As of now, the main rainfall is 
forecast from 1 AM to 6 AM with lingering showers that decrease 
in intensity and coverage through 1 PM.

Aside from the rainfall to start out tomorrow, dreary conditions 
will stick around and stymie our high temperature potential as 
values in the upper 60s to mid 70s are forecast.

Thursday and Beyond:

Southwesterly flow aloft is set to continue through the
remainder of the week and upcoming weekend, with a cooler lean 
to forecast highs than what is usually on deck for the time of 
year (80 for Omaha). Another nighttime swath of showers and 
storms is on deck to develop during the early hours of Thursday 
morning as the LLJ noses into north-central Kansas/southern 
Nebraska, trekking over the same areas that have gotten recent 
rainfall. This environment has lower potential in terms of 
rainfall rates, making flood chances lower but still possible. 
During the day Thursday, we'll see a widespread mass response to
the east of a deepening surface low over eastern Colorado that 
will help push temperatures aback into the upper 70s, only to be
improved further Friday for our one day of above-average high 
temperatures. 

That surface low is expected to eject off to the northeast Friday, 
developing a focused area of precipitation to its eastern and 
northeastern flanks (both of which are forecast to be largely north 
of the forecast area). What will move through our area will be a 
morning warm front that shoots north, with a dryline/surface trough 
that will stretch from the surface low over eastern SD towards 
western KS. This could have enough convergence along it to create 
some very high-base storms that would carry wind potential during 
the afternoon/early evening hours, with development much farther 
east towards the increasingly moist airmass looking unlikely. Over 
the course of the evening and heading into early Saturday, the main 
cold front will push into the area from the northwest, timing out 
poorly for severe weather watchers across the area. Nevertheless, 
another shot at moisture for wet areas could lead to some 
localized flooding threat with other hazards looking unlikely. 

The winds of change brought in by the cold front should take 
temperatures in a refreshing direction, with highs in the 70s 
Saturday falling further to near 70 Sunday and slightly cooler still 
Monday. Another shot at rainfall will arrive during this period as a 
shortwave trough traverses the northern two tiers of CONUS states 
while dragging forcing through the forecast area to create 
additional shots at rainfall. This again does not appear to be 
particularly potent rainfall at face value, but wet soils brings in 
a low end chance for hydro issues. At the moment the middle of the 
upcoming week is looking a bit drier, but rainfall won't be too far 
away as we transition from southwesterly flow to zonal flow aloft.
